subtopic_detail: Confirming central precocious puberty in a girl with accelerated growth
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6 year 8 month old girl whose mother noticed breast development about eight months ago that has steadily progressed. The school nurse has commented that she has shot up and now stands taller than every child in her class.

Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 91st centile over eighteen months. She has Tanner stage 3 breast development and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, with no clitoromegaly, no acne and no rapid deepening of her voice. Her mother reports no headache, no vomiting and no change in vision, and there are no cafe au lait patches on her skin. A bone age radiograph is advanced by two years.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 3 breast, Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, no virilisation, normal visual fields to confrontation, no skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Height crossed from the 50th to the 91st centile in eighteen months, bone age advanced by two years

lead_in: Which investigation will best establish the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary
options.rationale: Intracranial imaging is mandatory in boys and in girls under 6 years or with neurological features, but in a girl of this age with no such features it follows rather than precedes confirmation that the axis is centrally driven (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Measure dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and 17 hydroxyprogesterone levels
options.rationale: These adrenal androgen precursors are measured when virilisation dominates, and the picture here is oestrogenised with breast development and no clitoromegaly or acne (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to measure ovarian and uterine volumes
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound supports oestrogen exposure and can identify an ovarian cyst or tumour, but a pubertal uterus is a downstream finding that cannot distinguish central from peripheral drive (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Repeat the bone age radiograph in six months before any further testing
options.rationale: Serial bone ages are used to follow tempo in slowly progressive variants, and repeating one here wastes six months of predicted adult height in a rapidly advancing case (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Perform a gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test now
options.rationale: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation confirms central activation of the axis and separates it from gonadotrophin independent causes, which is the branch point for treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty; APEG clinical guidance on precocious puberty).
source_refs: APEG clinical guidance on precocious puberty

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty is defined in Australian practice as secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys, and the first task is always to separate central from peripheral causes because the treatments are entirely different. Central disease responds to gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonists that desensitise the pituitary, while peripheral disease requires removal or blockade of an autonomous oestrogen or androgen source. The stimulation test is the reference standard because a single random luteinising hormone can be misleadingly low early in the process. Untreated rapidly progressive central puberty closes the epiphyses early and costs adult height, which is why tempo and bone age advancement drive the decision to treat.
key_points: Precocious puberty means breast development before 8 years in girls
The first branch point is central versus peripheral, not benign versus malignant
A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation confirms central activation
Brain imaging is mandatory in all boys and in girls under 6 years
Rapid tempo with advanced bone age is what threatens adult height
explanation.pearls: Isolated premature thelarche in a toddler has a normal growth velocity and a bone age within six months of chronological age, and this combination reliably separates it from true central precocious puberty without any hormonal testing.

sources.label: APEG clinical guidance on precocious puberty

subtopic_detail: Raised intracranial pressure presenting as headache previously labelled migraine
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 6 year old boy brought in by his mother, who is frustrated that nothing has helped. For six weeks he has woken at about five in the morning with a headache and has vomited soon after, then felt well enough for school by mid morning. He was diagnosed with migraine four weeks ago and started on regular preventive medication with no change.

Over the past week he has been seeing double when he looks to the left, and his mother says he has become wobbly and grabs the furniture when he turns around. He is afebrile with no neck stiffness and no rash. Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins with loss of venous pulsation in both eyes, and his gait is wide based with a tendency to fall to the right.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 112/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Bilateral blurred disc margins, left abducens palsy, wide based ataxic gait, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure now
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in the presence of papilloedema with focal signs risks fatal tonsillar herniation and must never precede imaging in this setting (Source: RCH CPG: Headache).

options.text: Start regular propranolol for migraine and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Early morning headache with vomiting, a new cranial nerve palsy and ataxia are exclusion criteria for a primary headache diagnosis, and further preventive therapy would delay the diagnosis again (Source: RCH CPG: Headache).

options.text: Arrange urgent neuroimaging before any lumbar puncture is done
options.rationale: Papilloedema with a false localising abducens palsy and cerebellar signs indicates raised intracranial pressure, and urgent imaging both defines the lesion and determines whether cerebrospinal fluid sampling is ever safe (Source: RCH CPG: Headache; Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours

options.text: Refer to ophthalmology for formal visual field assessment first
options.rationale: Formal perimetry documents the consequence of raised pressure but does not identify its cause, and arranging it introduces a delay measured in days (Source: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone and review the headache tomorrow
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do reduce peritumoural oedema but are given after the lesion is identified and in consultation with neurosurgery, since blind use can obscure the diagnosis of a central nervous system lymphoma (Source: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours

explanation.summary: Childhood brain tumours are frequently preceded by weeks of headache attributed to migraine or viral illness, and the diagnostic delay in Australia averages several months. The pattern that should end that delay is headache with vomiting that is worse on waking and eases through the day, accompanied by any new neurological sign. An abducens palsy is the classic false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure because the long intracranial course of the sixth nerve makes it vulnerable regardless of tumour site. Posterior fossa tumours dominate in this age group, so ataxia and gait change carry particular weight, and imaging must precede any consideration of lumbar puncture.
key_points: Early morning headache with vomiting that eases by mid morning suggests raised pressure
A migraine diagnosis is unsafe in the presence of any new neurological sign
Abducens palsy is a false localising sign and does not indicate a brainstem lesion
Papilloedema with focal signs contraindicates lumbar puncture until imaging is done
Posterior fossa tumours are the commonest intracranial tumours of childhood
explanation.pearls: In a child under 2 years, crossing head circumference centiles with sunsetting eyes and a bulging fontanelle replaces papilloedema as the sign of raised intracranial pressure, because open sutures allow the head to expand before the discs swell.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Recognition of Childhood Brain Tumours

subtopic_detail: Parapneumonic effusion complicating community acquired pneumonia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl who was diagnosed with pneumonia five days ago and started on oral amoxicillin by her general practitioner. Her mother says the fevers have not settled at all, she is breathing faster than before and she now refuses to lie flat.

She is drinking about half her usual amount and has had three wet nappies today. On examination there is reduced chest expansion on the right with stony dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the lower half of that side. A chest radiograph shows homogeneous opacification of the lower right hemithorax with blunting of the costophrenic angle and a meniscus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 46, SpO2 92 per cent on room air, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Reduced right chest expansion, stony dullness at the right base, absent breath sounds over the lower right hemithorax, mild subcostal recession
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5); chest radiograph shows a right pleural effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics and arrange a chest ultrasound scan
options.rationale: Failure of oral therapy with an effusion requires intravenous cover for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, and ultrasound is the imaging of choice because it quantifies the fluid and shows septation that predicts the need for drainage (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest with intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Computed tomography adds radiation and often sedation without outperforming ultrasound for detecting loculation, and it is reserved for suspected necrotising pneumonia or an unclear anatomical picture (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia).

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter in the emergency department immediately
options.rationale: Drainage is often needed but the decision and the technique depend on whether the collection is free flowing or septated, which is exactly what the ultrasound determines first (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia).

options.text: Continue oral amoxicillin and repeat the chest radiograph in 48 hours
options.rationale: Persisting fever beyond 48 hours of appropriate oral therapy defines treatment failure, and continuing the same route in a hypoxic child with an effusion allows empyema to organise (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Perform a diagnostic pleural tap and send the fluid for cytology only
options.rationale: Any pleural sample in this setting must go for Gram stain, culture and pneumococcal nucleic acid testing as well, since cytology alone will not identify the organism guiding therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia).

explanation.summary: Parapneumonic effusion complicates a small proportion of childhood pneumonia and should be suspected whenever fever persists beyond 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. Ultrasound has displaced computed tomography as the first imaging test because it is radiation free, needs no sedation, distinguishes free fluid from septated empyema and can mark a drainage site at the bedside. Small free flowing collections often resolve on intravenous antibiotics alone, whereas septated collections generally require chest tube drainage with intrapleural fibrinolysis or video assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Long term lung function after treated childhood empyema is usually normal, which is worth telling frightened families early.
key_points: Fever beyond 48 hours on appropriate antibiotics signals a complication, most often an effusion
Ultrasound distinguishes free fluid from septation and guides drainage
Small free flowing effusions may resolve with intravenous antibiotics alone
Septated empyema needs drainage with fibrinolysis or surgical decortication
Pleural fluid goes for Gram stain, culture and nucleic acid testing
explanation.pearls: Send pleural fluid for pneumococcal polymerase chain reaction as well as culture, since culture is negative in most children already given antibiotics while nucleic acid testing still identifies Streptococcus pneumoniae and its serotype.

subtopic_detail: Inattention driven by sleep disordered breathing rather than attention deficit
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old boy whose mother brings a letter from his teacher describing him as fidgety, unable to finish tasks and drifting off during reading. She has read about attention difficulties and asks you to start medication before the next school term.

At home he snores loudly most nights, sleeps with his mouth open and his mother has watched him stop breathing and then gasp several times. He wakes unrefreshed and complains of a headache before breakfast two or three mornings a week. His concentration difficulties were first raised eight months ago when he started grade two and were not present in his preschool reports. His tonsils are large and nearly touching in the midline, and his growth has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils grade 3 with near midline contact, adenoidal facies with mouth breathing, no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile over twelve months, no sleep study or rating scales completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start immediate release methylphenidate and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: A stimulant trial cannot be a diagnostic shortcut when the inattention has an untreated organic explanation, and it will further disturb sleep and appetite in a child already losing weight (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Complete Conners rating scales and start atomoxetine if these are positive
options.rationale: Rating scales cannot distinguish attention deficit from sleep related inattention because both produce identical teacher reported items, and treating on that basis mislabels a reversible problem (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer for cognitive assessment to exclude a specific learning disorder
options.rationale: Formal cognitive testing is valuable when academic difficulty persists after sleep and hearing are optimised, but performing it while the child is chronically sleep deprived produces an artificially low result (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Refer for ear nose and throat review of sleep disordered breathing
options.rationale: Witnessed apnoeas with snoring, morning headache, faltering growth and grade 3 tonsils describe obstructive sleep apnoea, and adenotonsillectomy improves both the breathing and the daytime behaviour in a substantial proportion of these children (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea; Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Advise a trial of dietary elimination and review him in three months
options.rationale: Elimination diets have minimal effect on attention symptoms and carry nutritional risk in a child whose weight centile is already falling (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder requires symptoms present before 12 years, in two or more settings, and not better explained by another condition, and that last clause carries most of the diagnostic work in general practice. Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea produces hyperactivity and inattention rather than the sleepiness seen in adults, so it is one of the great mimics. The supporting features here are physiological rather than behavioural, with witnessed apnoeas, morning headache from overnight hypercapnia, faltering growth and obstructing tonsils. Adenotonsillectomy remains the first line treatment in Australian children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, and behavioural gains are often reported within months.
key_points: Attention symptoms must be present in two or more settings and not better explained otherwise
Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea presents as hyperactivity rather than sleepiness
Morning headache and faltering growth support overnight hypoventilation
Adenotonsillectomy is first line where adenotonsillar hypertrophy is present
Reassess attention formally once the sleep disorder is treated
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child sleeps with the neck hyperextended or sits up to breathe, since these positional adaptations are more specific for significant obstruction than snoring alone, which occurs in about one in ten well children.

sources.label: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Atypical curve features in an adolescent presenting with scoliosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner assessing a 12 year old girl whose mother noticed that one shoulder blade sticks out when she leans forward to wash her hair. She reports occasional back discomfort that sometimes wakes her at night.

On the forward bend test there is a rib hump on the left side of the thoracic spine. Her feet have high arches with clawed toes that her mother says have always looked that way. Abdominal reflexes are present in all four quadrants on the left but absent on the right. She has reached menarche and her lower limb power, tone and sensation are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Left sided thoracic rib hump on forward bending, bilateral pes cavus with clawing, absent right sided abdominal reflexes, symmetrical limb power

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a standing whole spine radiograph and review in six months
options.rationale: Radiographs measure the Cobb angle and are needed, but scheduling a routine six month review ignores the neurological findings that point away from idiopathic disease (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine urgently
options.rationale: A left sided thoracic curve, night pain, pes cavus and asymmetrical abdominal reflexes are the recognised atypical features that mandate neuroaxis imaging for syringomyelia, tethered cord or a Chiari malformation (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis; RCH CPG: Scoliosis).

options.text: Refer for a thoracolumbosacral orthosis to be fitted for her now
options.rationale: Bracing is offered for progressive idiopathic curves between about 25 and 40 degrees in a skeletally immature patient, and it does not treat a curve driven by an underlying cord abnormality (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis).

options.text: Reassure and repeat the forward bend test at the next school check
options.rationale: Watchful waiting applies to a small right sided thoracic curve with a normal neurological examination, and night pain with reflex asymmetry falls outside that group (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis).

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a scoliosis specific exercise program
options.rationale: Scoliosis specific exercises are an adjunct in mild idiopathic curves and would delay identification of a structural cord lesion by months (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis).

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a diagnosis of exclusion that classically produces a painless right sided thoracic curve in a girl around puberty with an entirely normal neurological examination. A curve that deviates from that template should raise the possibility of an underlying neuroaxis abnormality, and the traditional teaching that a left thoracic curve is atypical remains clinically useful. Absent or asymmetrical abdominal reflexes are the single most sensitive bedside sign of syringomyelia in this setting and are easily missed if not tested. Identifying a syrinx or tethered cord before surgery matters because correcting the curve without addressing the cord risks neurological injury.
key_points: Idiopathic curves are typically right sided, thoracic and painless
Left thoracic curves, night pain and rapid progression are atypical features
Absent or asymmetrical abdominal reflexes suggest syringomyelia
Pes cavus and clawed toes suggest an underlying neurological disorder
Neuroaxis imaging precedes bracing or surgical planning in atypical curves
explanation.pearls: A Cobb angle of 45 to 50 degrees in a skeletally immature adolescent is the usual threshold for surgical referral, while bracing is offered between roughly 25 and 40 degrees and does nothing once growth is complete.

subtopic_detail: Appendicitis masquerading as gastroenteritis in a preschool child
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 4 year old boy with three days of tummy ache. His father says the pain started around the belly button, and that since yesterday he has vomited five times and passed several loose stools, so the family assumed he had caught the gastro going around childcare.

He has not eaten since yesterday and has had one wet nappy today. He lies very still on the trolley and walks bent forward with small steps when asked to move. His abdomen is rigid in the right lower quadrant with involuntary guarding and he cries when the trolley is knocked. No other child at his centre has been unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Involuntary guarding and rigidity in the right lower quadrant, pain on percussion, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 168 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral rehydration solution and reassess the abdomen in four hours
options.rationale: Serial observation is a legitimate strategy for equivocal abdominal pain, but involuntary guarding with percussion tenderness indicates peritonism that will not be clarified by another four hours (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound before making any surgical referral
options.rationale: Ultrasound helps when the diagnosis is uncertain, and a non visualised appendix is common in a distressed child, so imaging must not delay referral once peritonism is established (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

options.text: Start intravenous fluids and refer urgently to the surgical team
options.rationale: Peritonism with tachycardia and delayed capillary refill after three days of symptoms indicates probable perforation, and resuscitation with a 20 mL per kg bolus alongside immediate surgical referral and antibiotics is the priority (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Send stool for culture and start oral metronidazole empirically today
options.rationale: Loose stools occur in perforated appendicitis from pelvic irritation of the rectum, and treating this as infective gastroenteritis is the classic error that delays diagnosis in preschool children (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen with oral contrast today
options.rationale: Computed tomography is avoided as a first line test in children because of radiation exposure, and ultrasound is the preferred modality when imaging is genuinely needed (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

explanation.summary: Appendicitis in children under 5 years carries a perforation rate above fifty per cent because the presentation is atypical and the omentum is too short to wall off the infection. Diarrhoea, vomiting and low grade fever lead families and clinicians toward gastroenteritis, and the discriminating features are the sequence of pain preceding vomiting and the reluctance to move. A child who lies still, walks bent forward and reacts to the trolley being bumped is demonstrating peritonism as reliably as any formal rebound test, which is unkind and unnecessary in this age group. Once peritonism is present, imaging is a distraction and the priority is fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and surgical review.
key_points: Perforation is the rule rather than the exception in children under 5 years
Pain preceding vomiting distinguishes surgical pathology from gastroenteritis
Diarrhoea can arise from pelvic irritation by a perforated appendix
Reluctance to move and pain on jolting are reliable signs of peritonism
Peritonism means resuscitate, give antibiotics and refer rather than image
explanation.pearls: Ask the child to jump on the spot or to cough, because a positive response has a similar diagnostic accuracy to formally elicited rebound tenderness and spares them the pain of deep palpation and release.

subtopic_detail: Preconception antiepileptic optimisation in a woman on sodium valproate
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman who tells you she and her partner want to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that have been fully controlled for three years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily, and she drives to work each day.

She has no other medical history, takes no other medication and does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her cycles are regular and she has never been pregnant. She is not currently using contraception and asks what she should do before conceiving.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Seizure free for three years, no recent antiepileptic drug levels, not taking any supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her today?

options.text: Refer for specialist review to change the antiepileptic before conception
options.rationale: Sodium valproate carries a dose related risk of major congenital malformation of roughly ten per cent and of impaired neurodevelopment in around thirty to forty per cent, so a supervised change to levetiracetam or lamotrigine is arranged before pregnancy and never abruptly in the first trimester (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue the current dose and start folic acid 5 mg daily from now
options.rationale: High dose folate is indeed part of the plan for any woman on an antiepileptic, but it does not offset the neurodevelopmental risk of valproate and is not a substitute for changing the drug (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy).

options.text: Stop the antiepileptic now and reassess seizure control in six months
options.rationale: Uncontrolled generalised tonic clonic seizures threaten maternal life and foetal oxygenation and would also cost her licence, so withdrawal is a specialist decision made against a defined relapse risk rather than a preconception default (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy).

options.text: Add lamotrigine to the current regimen and reduce the dose slowly
options.rationale: Polytherapy raises malformation risk above either agent alone, and valproate also inhibits lamotrigine metabolism so the combination needs careful specialist dosing rather than a general practice addition (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Advise conception now with folic acid 500 micrograms daily
options.rationale: The standard 500 microgram dose is for women at low risk, whereas antiepileptic therapy places her in the high risk group requiring 5 mg daily for at least a month before conception (Source: RANZCOG: Pre Pregnancy Counselling).

explanation.summary: Preconception care is the only point at which antiepileptic teratogenicity can be meaningfully reduced, because organogenesis is largely complete before most women present in the first trimester. Sodium valproate is the outlier among the commonly used agents, with both structural malformation and dose dependent neurodevelopmental harm including reduced intelligence quotient and increased autism spectrum diagnoses. Levetiracetam and lamotrigine have the most reassuring pregnancy data and are the usual substitutes, but switching takes months of overlap and titration with confirmed seizure freedom before conception. Every woman of childbearing potential taking valproate should be within a pregnancy prevention framework with effective contraception and documented annual review.
key_points: Valproate carries about a ten per cent malformation risk and substantial neurodevelopmental risk
Any drug change is completed before conception, never abruptly in the first trimester
Levetiracetam and lamotrigine have the most favourable pregnancy safety data
Women on antiepileptics take folic acid 5 mg daily preconception
Polytherapy carries higher teratogenic risk than an equivalent single agent
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises steeply through pregnancy and levels can fall by more than half by the third trimester, so levels are monitored and the dose increased, then reduced within days of birth to avoid postpartum toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Levothyroxine adjustment for treated hypothyroidism in the first trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who has just discovered she is pregnant. Her last menstrual period places her at 7 weeks gestation and an early scan confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a foetal heart present.

She has autoimmune hypothyroidism diagnosed six years ago and has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily without change for the last two years, with a stable result at her annual check. She takes no other medication, is not on any iodine containing supplement and feels well with no palpitations, tremor or neck swelling. Her thyroid function was checked yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, no proptosis, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 6.8 mIU/L (first trimester target below 2.5); free thyroxine 11.2 pmol/L (10-20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current dose and recheck thyroid function at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Leaving a thyroid stimulating hormone of 6.8 mIU/L untreated through the first trimester exposes the foetus to inadequate maternal thyroxine at the point of maximum dependence on maternal supply (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy).

options.text: Measure thyroid peroxidase antibodies before changing the levothyroxine
options.rationale: Antibody status is already implied by her established autoimmune diagnosis and would not alter the immediate need to raise the dose (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy).

options.text: Reduce the dose because reference ranges fall in early pregnancy
options.rationale: The thyroid stimulating hormone reference range does fall in early pregnancy because chorionic gonadotrophin stimulates the thyroid, but that makes her result more abnormal rather than less (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy).

options.text: Increase the dose by about 30 per cent and recheck in four weeks
options.rationale: Thyroxine requirements rise by roughly a quarter to a third from early pregnancy because of increased binding globulin and placental deiodination, so the dose is increased promptly and thyroid function repeated every four weeks until stable (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine uptake scanning to clarify the cause
options.rationale: Radioiodine studies are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because the foetal thyroid concentrates iodine from around 12 weeks (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: The foetal thyroid does not produce hormone until around 12 weeks, so first trimester neurodevelopment depends entirely on transplacental maternal thyroxine. Maternal requirements rise from as early as 4 to 6 weeks because oestrogen driven thyroxine binding globulin increases the bound fraction and the placenta degrades thyroid hormone. Women already on levothyroxine are therefore counselled preconception to increase their dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, commonly by taking two extra tablets each week. Overt untreated hypothyroidism is associated with miscarriage, pre eclampsia, preterm birth and reduced childhood intelligence quotient, which is why the trimester specific targets are set well below the non pregnant range.
key_points: The foetal thyroid does not function before about 12 weeks
Levothyroxine requirements rise by roughly 25 to 30 per cent from early pregnancy
First trimester thyroid stimulating hormone should sit below 2.5 mIU/L
Repeat thyroid function every four weeks until stable then each trimester
Radioiodine imaging and therapy are contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Levothyroxine absorption is blocked by iron and calcium in pregnancy supplements, so it must be taken on an empty stomach at least four hours apart from the antenatal multivitamin or an apparent dose failure will follow.

subtopic_detail: Weight banded enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis after emergency caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric resident reviewing a 33 year old woman on the first morning after an emergency caesarean section performed at 39 weeks for failure to progress after fourteen hours of labour. Her baby is feeding well and she has not yet been out of bed because of pain.

Her booking body mass index was 36 kg/m2 and her weight this morning is 98 kg. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism and takes no regular medication. Her blood loss was 500 mL, her haemoglobin is stable and her platelet count and renal function are normal. The regional anaesthesia catheter was removed six hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Weight 98 kg, abdominal wound dry and intact, calves soft and non tender, mobilising only with assistance
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155); platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis to prescribe?

options.text: Start enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days
options.rationale: The 20 mg dose is reserved for women under 50 kg, and using it at 98 kg gives subtherapeutic anti Xa activity (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

options.text: Start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days
options.rationale: Forty milligrams is the standard dose for women between about 50 and 90 kg, and it underdoses a woman weighing 98 kg because prophylaxis is banded by actual body weight (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

options.text: Prescribe graduated compression stockings alone until she is discharged
options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis is an adjunct and is used alone only when heparin is contraindicated, which is not the case with normal platelets, normal renal function and a dry wound (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

options.text: Start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously twice daily for six weeks
options.rationale: Extended six week prophylaxis at higher intensity is reserved for women with prior venous thromboembolism or high risk thrombophilia, neither of which she has (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

options.text: Start enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean, obesity and reduced mobility give at least two risk factors so prophylaxis runs for seven days, and the 91 to 130 kg band takes 60 mg daily (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the postpartum period carries the highest daily risk of the whole reproductive cycle. Risk assessment is performed at booking, on any antenatal admission and again after birth, with the number of risk factors determining both whether prophylaxis is given and for how long. Emergency caesarean scores more heavily than an elective one, and obesity, immobility, age above 35, parity, pre eclampsia and prolonged labour all add. Dosing is banded by actual body weight rather than fixed, because obesity both increases the thrombotic risk and lowers the anti Xa level achieved by a standard dose.
key_points: Emergency caesarean plus one additional risk factor triggers at least seven days of prophylaxis
Enoxaparin prophylaxis is banded by actual body weight, not given as a fixed dose
The 91 to 130 kg band receives 60 mg daily
Six week prophylaxis is for prior thromboembolism or high risk thrombophilia
Mechanical prophylaxis alone is used when heparin is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Neuraxial catheters and low molecular weight heparin must be separated in time, with the first prophylactic dose given no sooner than four hours after catheter removal and the catheter not removed within twelve hours of a prophylactic dose.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and the Puerperium

subtopic_detail: Choice of technique when a woman requests permanent contraception
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34 year old woman in clinic who has three children, the youngest aged 4 years, and has decided she does not want any more pregnancies. She has used the combined oral contraceptive pill for years but now gets migraine with aura and has stopped it.

She has no significant medical history, has never had abdominal surgery and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. Her last cervical screening test was negative two years ago and her periods are regular and not heavy. She has read about several approaches and asks which operation you would recommend for her.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no surgical scars, normal bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening negative two years ago, pregnancy test negative today

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic tubal occlusion as a day case procedure
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic tubal implants have been withdrawn from the Australian market following concerns about pain, migration and reoperation rates, so this is no longer an available option (Source: RANZCOG: Sterilisation).

options.text: Recommend laparoscopic bilateral salpingectomy as the preferred method
options.rationale: Complete removal of both tubes gives the lowest failure rate, removes the site where most high grade serous ovarian cancers arise, and adds no significant morbidity over clip occlusion at the same operation (Source: RANZCOG: Sterilisation; Cancer Council Australia clinical guidance).

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic tubal occlusion using Filshie clips instead
options.rationale: Clip occlusion remains effective but carries a higher lifetime failure rate than salpingectomy and provides none of the ovarian cancer risk reduction, so it is now the second choice (Source: RANZCOG: Sterilisation).

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system for her instead
options.rationale: The intrauterine system matches sterilisation for effectiveness and suits migraine with aura, but it is reversible and time limited so it does not meet a clear request for a permanent method (Source: Family Planning Australia clinical guidance).

options.text: Defer the decision and review her again in twelve months time
options.rationale: Deferral is appropriate when a decision is made in the immediate postnatal period or under pressure, and neither applies to a settled decision four years after her last birth (Source: RANZCOG: Sterilisation).

explanation.summary: Female sterilisation has shifted in Australian practice from tubal occlusion to complete bilateral salpingectomy, driven by evidence that most high grade serous ovarian carcinoma originates in the distal fallopian tube. Counselling must cover permanence, the small but real failure rate, the higher proportion of failures that are ectopic, and the availability of equally effective reversible alternatives. Vasectomy is discussed as part of that counselling because it has a lower failure rate and far lower procedural risk than any abdominal operation, although the decision belongs to the couple. Regret is most strongly predicted by young age, decisions made at the time of birth and relationship change, so documenting the discussion matters.
key_points: Bilateral salpingectomy is now the preferred sterilisation technique
Salpingectomy reduces later high grade serous ovarian cancer risk
Hysteroscopic tubal implants are no longer marketed in Australia
Long acting reversible contraception matches sterilisation for effectiveness
Regret is predicted by young age and decisions made around the time of birth
explanation.pearls: Counsel that pregnancy after tubal sterilisation carries a disproportionately high chance of being ectopic, so any subsequent positive pregnancy test needs an early transvaginal ultrasound rather than routine antenatal booking.
